entries.title: Minors living alone on Ceuta's streets at risk of abuse
entries.summary: Several thousand unaccompanied minors have gathered in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave on the northern coast of Africa. Illness and abuse are rife, and the authorities admit they are overwhelmed.
entries.content:
August 18, 2026

Several thousand unaccompanied minors have gathered in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave on the northern coast of Africa. Illness and abuse are rife, and the authorities admit they are overwhelmed.

It's 8 a.m. at the Tarajal industrial park in the autonomous city of Ceuta. But there are no workers and truck drivers to be seen near the warehouses today. Instead, there are makeshift tents, some of them made out of cardboard, with mainly children and teenagers sleeping under dirty blankets.

According to certain estimates, there could be between 3,000 and 5,000 unaccompanied minors in Ceuta. Some are living on the streets because they cannot find a spot in one of the already overcrowded reception facilities in the enclave.

Amina (not her real name), a 14-year-old Moroccan girl, and her brother were among the 80,000 people who crossed the border into Spain from Morocco in late July. Though most of these have since left Ceuta, some 9,000 remain, according to the local authorities — and many are minors. "

What's worst is that we don't have toilets," said Amina. "We have to go somewhere in the bushes, but I don't dare go alone."

Close by is a Moroccan woman called Malika (also not her real name) who has spread out several blankets for herself and her four children. She told DW she was not making enough as a cleaning lady in Morocco, adding that she earned the equivalent of €7 ($8) per day.

"That's just not enough to provide for everyone," she said. "School will start again soon, and I don't have any money for books, nor even decent clothes for the children."

That's why she decided to take part in the mass crossing of the Spanish border last month when she read about it on social media. But now she doesn't know what to do.

"One child got sick. He had a high fever, but I couldn't get help anywhere," she said. In the end, she made compresses with water and vinegar to see if that would help.

But now she is particularly worried about her 12-and 14-year-old daughters, because the number of sexual assaults has risen sharply in the past week. Police are currently investigating at least 15 suspected cases of rape. The local authorities suspect the actual number of cases to be much higher.

Conditions particularly difficult for girls

Susana Ascaso, an emergency doctor at Ceuta University Hospital, said she had treated several young girls in recent days.

"Just yesterday, another 12-year-old came to the emergency room," she said. "She said that other migrants had harassed her and touched her inappropriately. She arrived here completely terrified and in tears. She was with a woman who had found her on the street. That woman saved the girl."

Ascaso said conditions were particularly difficult for "girls under 18" who were "particularly at risk." She added that there was a major imbalance in the numbers of male and female migrants. "That doesn't help, of course."

Several high-ranking politicians in Ceuta have called for more support from the central government in the Spanish capital, Madrid. Nabila Benzina, the regional minister for health and social affairs, told DW that the current crisis was the "worst moment in Ceuta's history" and said more police officers were needed in the enclave. "Especially to protect young women, but also for the general protection of the population."

Ceuta's president, Juan Jesus Vivas, spoke of a "high-risk situation," in which it was increasingly difficult to maintain public services. "As far as minors are concerned, we are currently 5,000% over capacity," he said. "That means nobody can look after them adequately."

'I'd like to be an architect one day'

The Spanish government has announced plans to transfer unaccompanied minors to the mainland but there is no concrete timeline. Several regions, in which the far-right Vox party is part of the government, have said they refuse to take in any migrants.

Vivas told DW that the minors should be "reunited with their families. Otherwise, the Moroccan social services should assume responsibility for them." He said this was the only solution, adding that Madrid should put the "appropriate legal proceedings" in motion.

Many of the minors in Ceuta said they do not want to go back to Morocco or elsewhere in Africa despite the conditions in Ceuta.

Ibrahim, a 7-year-old child from Sudan, said he would not give up until he could provide "a better life for his parents back home." Amina, 14, also said she would not go back to Morocco.

"The schools here are really bad. I want a different future for myself. I'd like to become an architect someday," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Nigeria: Dozens killed in Plateau state attack
entries.summary: Officials in Nigeria have said at least 25 people were killed in their homes when armed men stormed their village Monday night. Fears of reprisal are real as violence between Muslim herders and Christian farmers spirals.
entries.content:
Africa

Nigeria: Dozens killed in Plateau state attack

August 18, 2026

Officials in Nigeria have said at least 25 people were killed in their homes when armed men stormed their village Monday night. Fears of reprisal are real as violence between Muslim herders and Christian farmers spirals.

Local officials say at least 25 people were murdered on Monday night by armed men who stormed the village of Bin-Per, in the Mangu local government area of Nigeria's Plateau state.

Perpetrators reportedly moved from house to house, killing residents with machetes.

Women and children accounted for most of the victims.

Resident Muftwan Yamput told France's AFP news agency that he and his family "survived by a whisker."

"But," he added, "my neighbors were attacked. Two people killed in their house."

Cycle of reprisals in Nigeria attacks

Monday night's massacre followed the killing of two herders last week.

Those were in turn followed by a suspected reprisal targeting the nearby village of Maitimbe, where multiple houses were torched.

The Mwaghavul Youth Movement, a local ⁠advocacy group, ​has accused authorities of ​failing to protect vulnerable communities.

"The ‌recurring destruction of communities, killing of innocent citizens, burning of homes and destruction of farmlands cannot continue ​to be treated ⁠as ordinary incidents," said the group's spokesperson on Sunday while calling for a review of security ​in the area.

Matthew Kwarpo, a representative in the Plateau state assembly, called on authorities to, "deploy proactive measures in preventing or mitigating unnecessary attacks before they occur," especially in Mangu.

"The incident underscores the urgent need for concerted efforts to address the underlying grievances and prevent further escalation of violence in the affected communities," said Kwarpo.

Amnesty says President Tinubu not fulfilling promise to 'enhance security'

The incidents of the last week are the continuation of years of spiraling violence between nomadic Muslim ethnic Fulani herders and mainly Christian farmers over access to increasingly scarce land and resources in central Nigeria's Middle Belt region.

Land grabbing over mineral and mining resources, political and economic tensions between locals and outsiders, and the influx of hardline Muslim and Christian preachers have all fueled divisions.

Plateau has also seen hundreds killed in urban riots between religious groups in recent years.

In May 2025, rights group Amnesty International (AI) estimated that at least 2,630 people had been killed in Plateau state alone in the two years since President Bola Tinubu had taken office on the promise of enhancing security.

The group said authorities had instead failed "to protect the rights to life, physical integrity, liberty and the security of tens of thousands of people across the country."

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Middle East: No talks or conversations with Iran, Trump says
entries.summary: Trump also claimed that the Strait of Hormuz was "open and operating," contrary to Iranian reports. Meanwhile, Syria, the US and Turkey condemned Israeli strikes on a Syrian airbase. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Iran

Middle East: No talks or conversations with Iran, Trump says

Published August 18, 2026last updated August 18, 2026

Trump also claimed that the Strait of Hormuz was "open and operating," contrary to Iranian reports. Meanwhile, Syria, the US and Turkey condemned Israeli strikes on a Syrian airbase. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Trump says 'no talks or conversations' between the US and Iran are held or scheduled
  • Syria, US, Turkey condemn Israeli strikes in Idlib
  • HRW says UN peacekeepers must remain in Lebanon

Read below for a roundup of the latest headlines on the Iran war and other developments in the Middle East region on Tuesday, August 18, 2026.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Israeli military acknowledges marking detained Palestinians with numbers

Israeli military acknowledges marking detained Palestinians with numbers

The Israeli military on Tuesday acknowledged that soldiers carrying out a raid in the northern West Bank on Monday had marked detained Palestinians with numbers.

In a statement to The Times of Israel newspaper, the military said the seriousness of the conduct had been stressed to the troops involved and that "lessons have been learned."

Footage emerged on Monday showing a Palestinian man speaking to local media after being questioned by Israeli soldiers, with the number 44 written across his forehead.

The man said the troops had marked others who were questioned.

The measure has long been considered taboo in Israel, as it is reminiscent of the numbered tattoos which Germany's Nazi regime used to identify concentration and death camp inmates during the Holocaust.

Earlier in April, footage showed Palestinian women with numbers written on their hands after they were briefly allowed to enter the Israeli military-controlled Jenin refugee camp to collect their belongings.

In response to the footage, the Israeli military acknowledged the incident and said "lessons have been learned," echoing a similar statement to the one issued on Tuesday.

Skip next section HRW calls on UN to keep international force in Lebanon

HRW calls on UN to keep international force in Lebanon

Human Rights Watch has called on the United Nations to keep its international peacekeepers' force in Lebanon, whose mandate ends this year.

The UNIFIL in southern Lebanon has been in place since 1978 to confirm Israeli withdrawal from the Arab country. It has some 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries.

Despite its presence, Lebanon has seen various wars between Israel and the pro-Iranian Hezbollah group, as well as Israeli ground invasions.

In August last year, the UN Security Council decided to end UNIFIL's mandate on December 31, 2026, amid growing US pressure.

"Pulling the plug on UNIFIL without a robust international force in place would effectively abandon millions of Lebanese civilians to an uncertain and potentially disastrous fate," said Louis Charbonneau, HRW's UN director said in a statement issued last week. 

"The peacekeepers are a crucial deterrent against attacks on civilians and human rights abuses," he added.

HRW argued that since the decision to end UNIFIL's mandate preceded this year's war and the subsequent Israeli invasion of southern Lebanon, the decision should be revised.

Hezbollah dragged Lebanon into the wider Middle East conflict on March 2 when it attacked Israel, in retaliation for US and Israeli attacks on Iran. This led to a wide Israeli bombing campaign and a ground invasion which has killed over 4,300 people in Lebanon.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun had last month also called on UNIFIL to stay beyond their mandate.

Skip next section UAE warns residents of 'potential missile threats'

UAE warns residents of 'potential missile threats'

The United Arab Emirates on Tuesday issued a brief phone alert for "potential missile threats," in the first such alarm since July.

"Due to the current situation, potential missile threats, immediately seek a safe place in the closest secure building," the Interior Ministry said in the phone alert, which was lifted shortly after.

The Ministry of Defense confirmed it had detected missiles "directed toward the country" for the first time in months.

At various points in the Iran war, and especially in the early days, UAE sites were the target of Iranian missile and drone strikes, in retaliation for US and Israeli strikes on Iran.

Skip next section 'Few tons of nuclear material' found in Syria, IAEA says

'Few tons of nuclear material' found in Syria, IAEA says

Rafael Grossi, the head of the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency said on Tuesday that the nuclear watchdog has found several tons of nuclear materials at a previously undeclared site in Syria which date back to ousted President Bashar Assad.

"After your courageous decision to inform us that there was another place, another site where nuclear material had been stored, we were able to access this place... we are talking about a few tons of nuclear material that could be put to bad use," Grossi told a news conference in Damascus.

Syria's foreign minister said the material was not dangerous and would remain in Syrian custody, subject to IAEA guarantees.

Speaking alongside Grossi in the press conference, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani said Syria had the right to use the material for civil and peaceful purposes.

Syria's interim government has committed to working with the IAEA to address the ousted regime's legacy of nuclear activities.

Skip next section Syria, US condemn Israeli strikes on military base

Syria, US condemn Israeli strikes on military base

Eight Israeli airstrikes hit an unused airbase in northwestern Syria's Idlib province early on Tuesday, Syrian state media reported, in attacks widely condemned by Damascus and Washington.

The attacks struck the runway and storage facilities at Abu al-Duhur base, Syrian state-run broadcaster Al-Ikhbariya reported, some 70 kilometers (43.5 miles) from the Turkish border.

Turkey is a key ally of Syria's interim government, in power since ousting former President Bashar Assad in a December 2024 lightning offensive.

Read our full report on the Israeli strikes here.

Skip next section 'No talks or conversations' with Iran, Trump says

'No talks or conversations' with Iran, Trump says

US President Donald Trump stressed on Tuesday that no talks or conversations between Washington and Tehran were being held or were scheduled.

"The Naval Blockade remains in full force and effect," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, claiming that the strategic Strait of Hormuz is "open and operating," in contradiction to Iranian reports.

"All water mines have been removed or detonated," Trump said of the strait, through which a fifth of the world's oil transited before the war began in late February.

Trump's latest statement came after a 60-day negotiating period between the US and Iran ended with no clear resolution, causing stock markets to largely fall and interest rates to spike on Tuesday.

Earlier on Tuesday, the British military's UK Maritime Trade Operations center reported that a projectile hit a ship as it sailed out of the Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Thank you for joining us as we bring you the latest on the situation in the Middle East, where US President Donald Trump has once again dismissed any potential breakthrough in negotiations with Iran, saying no talks or conversations are currently going on.

This comes a day after his son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner was in Israel, discussing with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ways to advance Trump's peace plan in Gaza.

On Tuesday, Israel struck a military airbase in Syria, drawing condemnation from Washington.

Elsewhere in the region, Human Rights Watch is warning of the planned withdrawal of UN peacekeeping troops from Lebanon after their mandate expires this year.

entries.title: Afghanistan: Only 5% of labor market are women under Taliban
entries.summary: The International Labour Organization estimates that only 5.1% of workers in Afghanistan are women, five years after the Taliban's return to power. That's less than a third of the proportion in 2019 and 2020.
entries.content:
Afghanistan

Afghanistan: Only 5% of labor market are women under Taliban

August 18, 2026

The International Labour Organization estimates that only 5.1% of workers in Afghanistan are women, five years after the Taliban's return to power. That's less than a third of the proportion in 2019 and 2020.

The share of women in Afghanistan's labor market has falled to around one worker in 20 in the five years since the Taliban returned to power, according to a report published by the International Labour Organization (ILO) on Tuesday. 

"Afghanistan is estimated to have the second lowest female labor force participation rate worldwide, at only 5.1% in 2026, against the backdrop of severe restrictions in women's access to education and employment," the ILO wrote.

It called for urgent steps to counter women's "severe exclusion," also saying this was essential to buttress the Afghan economy's resilience more generally. 

The Taliban rapidly returned to power in August 2021 amid a pullout by the US and other NATO forces, ending a 20-year period when women enjoyed comparatively improved economic and educational liberty after years of hardline Islamist rule.

What did the ILO say about women in Afghanistan's labor market?

The UN organization warned of "significant demographic and institutional changes" in the labor market since 2021, many of them disadvantaging women.

  • Female labor force participation had dipped from 16.5% in 2020 to 5.1% in 2026
  • That's the second lowest rate on the planet, only ahead of wartorn Yemen
  • Young women "NEETs" — people "not in education, employment or training" — represented 84% of the cohort, compared to 76% in 2020 and 68% in 2019
  • Among young men, the NEET figure was below 30%, and falling compared to the recent high-point of the COVID pandemic in 2020
  • The UN's Development Agency meanwhile said one rare boom area was businesses owned by women
  • These had increased in prevalence roughly tenfold, albeit precisely because other employment options were so scarce

"Afghanistan cannot build a resilient labor market while such a large share of its population remains excluded from economic activity," said Tite Habiyakare, senior coordinator and head of the ILO office for Afghanistan.

What did the ILO say about Afghanistan's economy more generally?

The report said that Afghanistan's labor market remained "under considerable pressure" five years after the Taliban takeover, having only moderately recovered from the crash of 2021.

Afghanistan's GDP tumbled by around 15% when the Taliban returned amid the COVID pandemic and western troops and funds flowed out. It remained deep in negative territory in 2022 and had just barely clawed its way into positive growth territory since, falling well short of returning to its pre-Taliban levels.

Employment numbers have started to rise in absolute terms, but not fast enough to keep up with population growth — either domestic or as a result of emigrant returns — meaning the share of people in work is flatlining at just under one-third of the population.

The paper also called for increased investment in representative labor force data-gathering, warning that its data was reliant on modeling estimates that "are subject to considerable uncertainty and should be interpreted with appropriate caution."

How are external factors like the war in Iran and migrant returns impacting the situation?

Large-scale returns of emigrants, particularly from Iran and Pakistan, have become "one of the defining labor market challenges facing Afghanistan," the report said.

More than 6 million Afghans returned from Iran and Pakistan between 2023 and the end of May this year, with the surge driven "by a combination of policy, economic and security factors."

The report noted World Bank projections suggesting that this could halve the influence of remittance inflows into the Afghan economy, from around 4% of GDP in 2020 to around 2% of economic output by 2025.

"Since February 2026, the Middle East crisis has added further uncertainty for Afghans residing in Iran, alongside the continued implementation of returns policies," the ILO said. 

Finally, the ILO warned that the war in Iran posed additional risks for Afghanistan — in terms of general inflation, food and fuel prices, trade and transport disruptions, and increased potential returns from Iran. 

Around 70% of workers, partiularly less skilled ones, were at least moderately exposed to factors relevant to the crisis like energy prices, the report found, with roughly 30% facing only slight exposure.

It noted a steep rise in inflation figures in the past 12 months, rising from less than 1% in May 2025 to around 8% by May 2026, and warned that such increases "disproportionately affect poorer households and reduce real earnings, particularly among informal workers."

entries.title: As drought hits Germany's harvest, will food prices rise?
entries.summary: Germany's main farmers' association has warned of a below-average harvest after drought and crops damaged by extreme heat. DW looks into what lower yields could mean for food prices and grocery bills.
entries.content:
August 18, 2026

Germany's main farmers' association has warned of a below-average harvest after drought and crops damaged by extreme heat. DW looks into what lower yields could mean for food prices and grocery bills.

1. How severe is Germany's 2026 harvest decline?

The German Farmers' Association (DBV) on Tuesday warned of a "below-average" harvest due to ongoing drought that has left large areas of farmland severely parched.

In a statement, DBV President Joachim Rukwied warned that the country's grain harvest would be 7% lower than last year, blaming an "overly dry spring and a heat wave in the second half of June," which had "significantly damaged many crops."

Overall grain production was expected to be 41.9 million tons this year, the DBV said, a shortfall of some 3.3 million tons compared with 2025.

Rapeseed saw the largest fall, with 3.3 million tons harvested, nearly 17% lower than last year. Barley remained at last year's level despite a lower yield, as more land was used to grow the crop.

The potato crop was also expected to be below average and some regions would see a "significantly worse" harvest for sugar beet, DBV said.

Rukwied noted how location played a bigger role in determining crop yields this year than usual, and pointed to poor crop yields and even crop failures, particularly in southern and western Germany.

Separately, Germany's Federal Statistical Office warned that the country's apple harvest was forecast to drop 18% compared with last year.

Germany is experiencing a severe drought during a summer of frequent record-breaking temperatures, which has exacerbated the effects of below-average rainfall since March, according to the German Weather Service.

2. How will the drought affect food prices and availability?

Agriculture Minister Alois Rainer said Tuesday that the government isn't expecting a sudden or sharp increase in food prices as a result of the lower harvest.

"I don't expect prices to rise immediately because food prices also depend on many other factors — the supply chain, transportation and production," he told public broadcaster ZDF.

The German Raiffeisen Association, which represents 1,600 agricultural cooperatives, also said last week a large hike in prices was unlikely.

However, the large falls in rapeseed and sugar beet production could reduce domestic supply of oil and sugar, requiring imports to make up the shortfall.

Local media reported last week that the drought was also causing animal feed stocks to fall drastically in several states, particularly in southern Germany.

The German Farmers' Association has previously warned that lower grain yields and weaker grassland growth could push up prices for feed, meat, milk and eggs

In the hardest-hit areas of the country, potatoes and other vegetables could become more expensive as supply tightens. For most shoppers, however, the main impact is more likely to be gradual price increases rather than shortages.

3. How does this drought fit into wider food security concerns?

Farming, both at home and globally, has faced repeated pressures since the COVID-19 pandemic.

German food prices have risen by over 36% since 2020, according to government data published last month.

The price hikes were especially strong for poultry meat, many dairy products and eggs, edible fats and oils, and sugar, the government calculated.

Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted Black Sea exports of Ukrainian grain in 2022 and drove energy prices higher, impacting the cost of fertilizer, transport and food processing.

More recently, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran war prevented oil, gas and fertilizer ingredients from leaving the Gulf.

The conflict has pushed up prices of diesel fuel, fertilizers and pesticides, with some farmers cutting back on soil nutrients.

Compounding crises over the past six years have left large parts of the German agriculture sector financially stretched, the industry has warned. Many farmers have said they face much higher costs and rising debts, and have limited room to absorb further losses.

4. What support are German farmers seeking?

The German Farmers' Association said some farmers may need interim financing to secure their futures. Rukwied called on Berlin to launch an "immediate package" to help support the agriculture sector.

Recommendations include boosting the European Union's fertilizer aid package from €60 million to €180 million ($208 million), paid out quickly and without red tape.

DBV also called on ministers to cut the tax on agricultural diesel, at least until the end of November.

For several months from late 2023, German farmers blocked highways with tractors over plans to scrap fuel subsidies for the agricultural sector, which were later partially reversed.

Agriculture Minister Rainer on Tuesday promised targeted help to farmers, but only when reliable official figures are available at the end of August.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: Dressed for power: Giorgia Meloni and the language of fashion
entries.summary: From Giorgia Meloni's shift from dark suits to pastels to Angela Merkel's signature jackets, politicians have long used clothing to shape how voters see them. In this day and age, power dressing has evolved.
entries.content:
August 18, 2026

From Giorgia Meloni's shift from dark suits to pastels to Angela Merkel's signature jackets, politicians have long used clothing to shape how voters see them. In this day and age, power dressing has evolved.

Often dressing in pastel colors, with wide-legged pants falling over her high heels, Italy's first female prime minister can't escape fashion scrutiny — and not only because Giorgia Meloni is the leader of the world's fashion capital.

"Fashion is a language — it tells us what its wearer wants to say without any actual words," Michela Bonafoni, who teaches fashion at Unicollege in Florence, told DW.



"Perhaps what you wear is very close to your personality. But if you want to give a different impression of yourself, you can also do this through clothing — this is what Meloni does constantly," explained Bonafoni.

Meloni's clothing style can be read as part of a broader political transition: from outsider to establishment figure. When she first took office in 2022, her appearance was closely tied to the political identity she had built as a leader of the right-wing Brothers of Italy party with post-fascist roots. Her look: dark suits with chunky boots, serious and even combative.

Enter the concept of "power dressing," which emerged in the 1970s and became influential in the 1980s, as second-wave feminism coincided with more women entering professional and managerial roles. The suit became a way for women to signal authority in traditionally male workplaces.

Italian designer Giorgio Armani played a key role — his softer, more fluid tailoring offered a new version of the power suit — borrowing from menswear while creating a more feminine language of authority.

During her first official public appearances, Meloni was often seen in dark Armani suits, a nod to traditional power dressing, and a look that said, according to Bonafoni: "I'm here in this kind of government and that's all there is to it."

From masculine suits to pastels

Since then, Meloni's look has softened — she's often seen in wide-legged silhouettes and suits in cream, beige, pink and other muted or pastel shades. The style change also coincides with how she has become a more established figure in European politics, moving closer to the European Union and becoming a prominent supporter of Ukraine.

Yet, Meloni has maintained a conservative approach to domestic politics, which hasn't gone down well with much of the public — including many in the country's fashion industry. No luxury brand, including Armani, has publicly stepped forward to style her or support her use of their clothing.

This hasn't stopped Meloni from using fashion to appeal to a broader public. "When Meloni understood that many Italians didn't like some of the actions of her government, she started to wear the pastel colors, which incite understanding and say 'I'm Giorgia, a woman who is kind,'" said Bonafoni. The author also pointed out that Meloni sports "Made in Italy" designers as part of her brand of nationalism — attaching its power to her own.

At the Salone del Mobile, Italy's premier design event in Milan this past April, Meloni chose an informal look: jeans and a casual beige blazer.

"Her look said: I'm casual because I'm just like you — but I'm also exactly where I want to be right now in this moment and in this government," said Bonafoni. Such a style exudes confidence and is closer to the more relaxed style of female politicians in the US, Bonafoni added.

A political 'uniform'

But political power doesn't always require a changing wardrobe. For some female leaders, consistency itself can become a form of power dressing.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel developed one of the most recognizable wardrobes in modern politics. Her formula was remarkably consistent: trousers and a three-button jacket, with the jackets appearing in an extraordinary range of colors. The simplicity itself became a kind of uniform, putting Merkel herself, as a politician, rather than her fashion, at the center.

"Her 'second skin' of clothing was very close to her character, her attitudes and political decisions she made," said Bonafoni.





Former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher also had her fashion uniforms so to speak, down pat. Her appearance was carefully constructed — tailored suits, pearls, handbags — an instantly recognizable version of feminine political authority in her era.

These days, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum offers another prime example of a politician who uses clothing to send a message. She frequently wears garments made by women artisans from Mexico to show her support and solidarity with Mexico's Indigenous communities.

From hipster dad to tactical wear

While the few women politicians we have on the world stage fall under increased fashion scrutiny, men too have long understood the political power of appearance — perhaps now more than ever. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy often chooses to wear tactical clothing that's far from the standard suit and tie look of most world leaders.

As Ukrainian journalist Illia Ponomarenko told Politico last year, it's part of his anti-elitist message, one that directly confronts the world leaders he meets. "His clothes are basically asking: What are you about? Are you about the business of saving lives, or are you about fancy protocols?" said Ponomarenko. "Even when he meets with kings, he dresses in a way that represents the average Ukrainian involved in this war effort. So it's a message to say, 'I've come to the corners of power as a representative of my humble people.'"



Similarly, the UK's Labour Party Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose look has been referred to as "hipster dad," chooses smart-casual styles; T-shirts, polo shirts and trainers. It's a political messaging move that says he's on the same level as the public. 



As for Giorgia Meloni, Bonafoni expects the world will soon see another style change as she is challenged by far-right politician and former army general Roberto Vannacci.

"Meloni has said she doesn't want Vannacci in her government, but her party will need him in a coalition if it wants to remain in power," said Bonafoni. "I'm sure if and when Vannacci challenges her, she will change her style again because she'll have to present herself as someone who's even more powerful."

Edited by: Tenzin Sekhon

entries.title: Syria, US condemn Israeli strikes on military base
entries.summary: Israel has not officially claimed the strikes on Abu al-Duhur airbase in Idlib, some 70 kilometers from the Turkish border. US envoy Tom Barrack called the Israeli strikes an "unnecessary escalation."
entries.content:
Syria

Syria, US condemn Israeli strikes on military base

August 18, 2026

Israel has not officially claimed the strikes on Abu al-Duhur airbase in Idlib, some 70 kilometers from the Turkish border. US envoy Tom Barrack called the Israeli strikes an "unnecessary escalation."

Eight Israeli airstrikes hit an unused airbase in northwestern Syria's Idlib province early on Tuesday, Syrian state media reported, in attacks widely condemned by Damascus and Washington.

The attacks struck the runway and storage facilities at Abu al-Duhur base, Syrian state-run broadcaster Al-Ikhbariya reported, some 70 kilometers (43.5 miles) from the Turkish border.

Turkey is a key ally of Syria's interim government, in power since ousting former President Bashar Assad in a December 2024 lightning offensive.

What else do we know about the Israeli airstrikes on the Idlib airbase?

Syrian state media, quoting a military source, said that "Israeli occupation aircraft early this morning targeted the runway" of the base "with eight strikes," damaging infrastructure but without causing casualties.

The facility has been out of service as a dedicated military base for over a decade. The Reuters news agency cited an unnamed military source as saying it has been used as a training center for Syria's new army since Assad's 2024 ouster.

Israel has yet to officially comment on the attacks.

They come on the heels of a Turkish military delegation's visit to the airfield, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights monitor. According to the UK-based monitor, the visit was part of efforts to reactivate the base.

How did the US, Syria react to the attacks?

Tom Barrack, US ambassador to Turkey and special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq, condemned the Israeli strikes in a post on X.

"We are deeply concerned that the confirmed Israeli airstrikes on Abu al-Duhur Airbase constitute an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability," Barrack wrote.

He defended Syria's interim administration of Ahmed al-Sharaa, who once led an Al-Qaeda-affiliated militant group but has since distanced himself from Islamist militancy. Barrack stressed Sharaa's administration "repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel."

"We encourage all parties to prioritize logical discourse over further military incidents," he said.

Syria's Foreign Ministry also condemned the strikes, calling them "an unjustified act of aggression."

It urged the international community and the United Nations Security Council to "take a firm position against Israel's repeated violations of Syrian sovereignty."

The "continuation of these Israeli attacks" since December 2024 came while Syria "has exercised restraint and worked to consolidate stability and avoid escalation," it added.

Turkey also strongly condemned the Israeli airstrikes, calling on "the international community to ⁠take ​a ​more decisive stance to ​end Israel's ‌escalating aggression against Syria."

Tense Israeli-Turkish relations overshadowed by Syria

Since Assad's ouster, Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria, sending troops to a United Nations-patrolled buffer zone that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in Syria's Israeli-occupied Golan since 1974.

The Israeli army has also carried out regular incursions deeper inside Syrian territory.

Israeli officials have declared their intention to keep forces in a self-declared "security zone" in southern Syria.

Turkey has accused Israel of trying to destabilize Syria and its new administration, which Ankara has been helping by training its army and assisting with building its state institutions and infrastructure.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz has directly warned Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, stressing Israel would now allow steps that strengthen Syria's military capabilities in ways that could threaten Israel.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Should India be worried about the Mecca defense pact?
entries.summary: A defense agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey brings Islamabad deeper into the security architecture of the Middle East. How is India planning to respond?
entries.content:
India

Should India be worried about the Mecca defense pact?

August 18, 2026

A defense agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey brings Islamabad deeper into the security architecture of the Middle East. How is India planning to respond?

The "Mecca Joint Defense Agreement" signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on August 7, comes amid the Iran war and shifting security arrangements in the Middle East.

Saudi Arabia is seeking additional security partnerships as it faces uncertainty over the reliability of the US security umbrella. Turkey is seeking a larger regional role, while Pakistan is looking to turn its longstanding military relationship with Riyadh into wider strategic influence.

The agreement calls for collective defense, stating an armed attack on one member will be regarded as an attack on all three.

It also formalizes relationships that already exist. Pakistan has trained and assisted Saudi forces for decades, while its defense relationship with Turkey has expanded through military exchanges and cooperation.

For India, the question is whether the pact gives archrival Pakistan a deeper role in a region central to Indian interests.

Pact changes little on the ground for India

Some Indian analysts see little immediate change in the regional balance. Others see a warning that India needs a stronger security presence in a region where its economic interests have grown considerably.

Saudi Arabia is a major energy and investment partner for New Delhi. The Gulf and the Red Sea are vital to India's trade and energy security.

The pact allows Pakistan to expand on its security role in the Gulf while providing an institutional framework for closer defense cooperation and potentially greater access to funding and technology.

However, former Indian High Commissioner to Pakistan Ajay Bisaria believes the agreement will have little effect on the basic dynamics of an India Pakistan confrontation.

"The Mecca pact is not worth the paper it's written on," Bisaria told DW.

"It does little to move the needle beyond the Saudi-Pakistan defense pact of last year, an arrangement that proved to have only signaling value for Iran, the US and Israel, at a moment when Riyadh was unsettled by the frailty of the American security umbrella," he added.

In the event of a future India-Pakistan crisis, the former ambassador said he does not expect the pact to fundamentally alter Saudi Arabia's position.

"For India, this is a pact to be monitored, not one to be unduly concerned about," Bisaria said.

"In the event of another terrorist attack from Pakistan, the situation is unlikely to look very different from Operation Sindoor, save, perhaps, for some added rhetoric," he said, referring to the name of India's response to a 2025 attack on tourists in Kashmir that New Delhi has blamed on Pakistan-backed militants. Islamabad has denied any involvement in the attack.

"Turkey would continue to supply drones and equipment to Pakistan, while the Saudis, far from rushing to position themselves as its defenders, are more likely to offer their services, more vocally, as mediators," he said.

No immediate concern for India

Tara Kartha, former member of the National Security Council Secretariat, believes India should not overstate the significance of the agreement.

"India doesn't need to be overly concerned about the Mecca pact. Saudi Arabia and Turkey hardly see us as a strategic competitor or an 'enemy'," Kartha told DW.

Much of the Pakistan-Turkey military relationship already exists, Kartha added. "Turkey's formidable defense industry will certainly be made available for the pact's constituents," she said.

"But Pakistan and Turkey already have a strong defense relationship including joint development of the Kaan aircraft. So, nothing really changes on the ground barring possibly increased funding for the Pakistan defense budget. That is certainly a problem that can't be easily circumvented," she said.

The more immediate concern for India may be whether Saudi resources and Turkish technology could strengthen Pakistan's military capabilities over time.

India's ties with Saudi Arabia

Beyond the India-Pakistan rivalry, the pact also raises questions about India's ties with Saudi Arabia.

The kingdom has built a substantial relationship with India, spanning energy, investment, trade and political ties. And Riyadh's effort to diversify its security partnerships does not necessarily mean choosing Pakistan over India.

Geopolitical analyst Harsh Pant, vice president at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation, told DW that India should respond cautiously but not passively.

"The different strategic interests of the three members could limit the pact's cohesion, but New Delhi should use its own relationship with Riyadh to deepen security, intelligence and economic cooperation," Pant said.

Deeper bilateral ties with Saudi Arabia, he added, could help ensure that Pakistan's new role does not translate into disproportionate influence in the Gulf.

New Delhi will also have to watch the military dimension closely. If Turkish drones, missiles, electronic warfare systems or other defense technologies become more readily available to Pakistan, India's western security calculations could change.

A wake-up call for India?

Randhir Jaiswal, spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs, said New Delhi was examining the pact's implications "from the perspective of India's national security and considerations of regional peace and stability."

"India remains fully committed to safeguarding its national interests and will take all necessary measures in this regard," he said.

Strategic expert C. Raja Mohan told DW that the trilateral agreement points to a larger problem in India's approach to the Gulf. India's economic dependence on the region has grown considerably, while its security presence has remained comparatively limited, he said.

"For India, this should be a warning that New Delhi cannot remain primarily a diplomatic and economic player in the Gulf. It needs greater military reach in the region and deeper, practical security and defense relationships with individual Middle Eastern countries," Mohan said.

He sees a widening mismatch between India's interests and its security presence.

"The gap between India's economic interests and its limited military-security presence is becoming harder to ignore," he added.

India could deepen defense and intelligence cooperation with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, strengthen maritime security in the Arabian Sea and Red Sea, and closely monitor Pakistan-Turkey military cooperation.

Mohan, a professor of American Studies at Jindal Global University, sees the agreement principally as an attempt by Saudi Arabia to widen its options.

"I see it more as evidence of the Arab states' continuing inability to build a dependable regional security system and, importantly, as Saudi Arabia hedging against uncertainty over the reliability of the US security umbrella," Mohan said.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Fact check: How do I spot AI-generated images?
entries.summary: Images created or manipulated with artificial intelligence tools are flooding social media. How can you know what's real and what's not? Here are a few tips.
entries.content:
August 18, 2026

Images created or manipulated with artificial intelligence tools are flooding social media. How can you know what's real and what's not? Here are a few tips.

Anyone with an internet connection and access to an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can create photorealistic images within seconds, for free or for very little money, and then spread them on social networks at breakneck speed.  

The tools used to create AI-generated images are improving rapidly, reducing the number of obvious AI errors – often referred to as AI hallucinations – and making it increasingly difficult for users to determine whether a viral image depicts a real event.

Gone are the days when AI tools routinely produced images of public figures with four fingers, an excessive amount of teeth or unnatural body proportions.

An additional challenge is that while many images are entirely AI-generated, others are real photos that have been partially altered using AI.

Here's one example: an authentic broadcast image from the 2026 World Cup in which a fan was replaced by an Adolf Hitler lookalike.

Of course, the image was actually created using an OpenAI-powered tool.

So how can you spot AI-generated images? DW Fact check offers tips to help you navigate today's information landscape.

Look closely at the picture

You may remember the story of a Syrian teenager who helped stop a knife attack in the German city of Hamburg in 2025.  

As the story spread, conflicting accounts of the incident emerged on social media, along with AI-generated images like the one above.

The image looks authentic at first glance, but if you zoom in and examine it carefully, you'll find obvious inconsistencies.

That's why it's important to take your time and inspect the details. Common AI errors might be hidden in the background, including distorted objects and gibberish-filled text.

If your device doesn't allow you to zoom in far enough, online tools can help.

A tool we often use at DW Fact check is Forensically, a free online photo forensics platform that includes a magnifier and other features for examining images closely.  

Think about the context

Remember the Hitler lookalike from above? A supporter resembling the Nazi dictator would almost certainly have attracted immediate attention from broadcasters, stadium officials and other spectators.

Yet no reputable media organizations reported such a stir, and no fans in the stadium shared posts showing the lookalike from a different perspective.

This example highlights a key verification technique: move beyond the pixels and ask yourself whether the event itself makes sense.

One way of doing that is checking whether the apparent event has been covered by trustworthy news organizations.

If an image appears to show a highly unusual or controversial incident, but there is no evidence of it in credible reporting, that should raise a red flag.

You can also look at who's posting and sharing the image. If the account often shares AI-generated material or appears to have no connection to the event itself, it's wise to treat the image with caution.

Find the image source

If you're unsure whether an image is real or generated by AI, try to find its source.

One way to do this is by conducting a so-called reverse image search. Instead of searching with keywords, you can upload an image to tools like Google Imagesor TinEye. 

These tools can help answer several questions:

  • When was the image first uploaded?
  • On which platforms is the image being shared?
  • What are users saying about it in comments and posts?
  • Have any reputable fact-checkers already verified the image?

Of course, some AI-generated images may be brand new and therefore produce few or no results.

But manipulated images are often based on older, authentic pictures. In those cases, a reverse search can reveal the original image and provide important context.

If you find that an image has already been fact-checked, one way to assess the credibility of the article or video is to see whether the organization is certified by the International Fact Checking Network (IFCN).  

The IFCN assesses fact-checkers against a set of professional standards, which include being as fair and transparent as possible, being non-partisan, and committing to open and honest corrections.

You can find a list of IFCN-certified outlets here, including DW Fact check.

The IFCN should not be confused with the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN), a Russian platform with close ties to the Kremlin. 

Use AI tools with caution

AI detectors can help assess whether an image was created or modified using AI. They search for invisible watermarks and other digital traces associated with AI-generated content.

There are a few different types.

Tech companies such as Google and OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, have developed systems that identify whether their own AI models were used to create or modify an image.

Google's SynthID tool can be accessed here, and hereis the link to OpenAI's verification tool.

Other tools, such as Image Whisperer, AI or Not, and Hive Moderation, estimate the likelihood that an image was manipulated using AI.

And then AI chatbots, such as X's Grok, can provide answers to user questions on whether images are real or fake.

In the Hitler lookalike example, OpenAI identified a digital watermark, which confirmed it was manipulated using the AI company's tools.

One important word of caution: AI detectors often make mistakes.

Their findings should not be treated as definitive proof, but rather as one piece of the verification puzzle.

If possible, use more than one tool and cross-check the results to reduce the risk of drawing the wrong conclusions.

When in doubt, don’t share

Even after following all these steps, you may still be unsure whether an image is real or AI generated.

As AI technology continues to improve, distinguishing between authentic and AI-generated images is becoming increasingly difficult.

If you cannot verify an image with confidence, our recommendation is simple: don't share it, especially on social media.

Instead, consider warning friends and family members privately that the image's authenticity has not been confirmed and that it should be treated with caution.

And if you're still unsure, you can always send the image to us at factchecking@dw.com. We may be able to help verify its authenticity.

This article was first published in 2023 and has been revised to incorporate new developments and trends. Joscha Weber and Kathrin Wesolowski contributed to that report. Edited by Josh Axelrod.

 This article is part of a DW Fact check series on digital literacy. Other articles include:

  • How do I spot manipulated images?
  • How do I spot audio deepfakes?
  • How do I spot propaganda?
  • How do I spot fake social media accounts, bots and trolls?

And here you can read more about how DW fact-checks fake news.

entries.title: Designing food for a hotter world
entries.summary: Inside futuristic labs, plants are scanned, stressed and analyzed. The aim is to use the results to produce plant strains that can better serve a growing population in a warming world.
entries.content:
August 18, 2026

Inside futuristic labs, plants are scanned, stressed and analyzed. The aim is to use the results to produce plant strains that can better serve a growing population in a warming world.

Rows of tomato saplings stand in a room packed with cameras. Just a few weeks old, they're under constant surveillance as scientists monitor them for tiny changes in color, temperature and photosynthesis.

These plants are growing in a chamber designed to mimic the heat and humidity of India's climate. By analyzing their reactions to different stressors, researchers at Wageningen University in the Netherlands are aiming to uncover genetic traits that have the potential to make crops resilient to human-caused climate change.

"We can regulate the temperature. We can give them a heat stress phase, we can freeze shortly, so we can simulate night frost, which could be very disruptive for young plants," explained Rick van de Zedde, program manager at the Netherlands Plant Eco-phenotyping Centre (NPEC). "We can introduce salinity by adding salt."

In fact, the scientists can simulate almost any condition on the planet. "I would call it a gym for plants," said van de Zedde.

Why understanding plants is so important

This research is becoming ever more essential. Agriculture has traditionally relied on predictable seasons and conditions, with farmers planning around established weather patterns — planting in the spring and harvesting in the autumn, for example.



But as societies burn fossil fuels that heat the planet, rising global temperatures are disrupting that rhythm.

Increasing heat waves, longer and more intensive droughts and severe flooding caused by global heating is increasingly putting crops at risk.

Following soaring temperatures this summer, farmers in some regions of Germany are warning of harvest failure. Grain production losses have already been registered in countries including France, Hungary and the United Kingdom.

With the global population predicted to hit 10 billion by 2050, the pressure is on to produce enough food. That race is intensified by rising meat consumption, which implies growing more grain for animal feed.

Simultaneously, demand for crops to use as biofuels, which are made from organic material including plants or animal waste, is also on the rise.

For researchers, the question is no longer just how to grow more food, but how to do so under increasingly challenging conditions.

A high-tech way ahead

Dubbed the 'Silicon Valley' of agriculture, the Netherlands has long been a leader in farming innovation. Despite its relatively small size, the country is the world's second-largest exporter for agricultural products by value — after the US.

Inside the Wageningen University greenhouses, scientists recreate environmental conditions such as drought, tropical humidity or frosty nights, and use a range of technology to monitor the plants.

Over a period of weeks, automated scales record the weights of tree species every three minutes to reveal how much water they need. Sophisticated scanners track the movement of leaves as part of a process known as phenotyping — which measures plants and their features.



Though botanists have been tracking flora for thousands of years to select the best plants, the processes were historically manual and therefore slow and painstaking.

"All the lab measurements were restricting the size of the experiments," van de Zedde told DW. "If you look around here in NPEC, you see that we are talking about thousands of plants in one experiment."

Taking experiments into the field

Despite the sophistication of the lab, it cannot completely mirror real-world conditions. Factors like hailstorms, high winds or differing soil temperatures remain difficult to recreate.

Near the university, experimental barley fields provide an important reality check. It is there that researchers deploy mobile imaging and use GPS positioning systems to collect data on hundreds of crop varieties in the field.

By comparing greenhouse and field results, they are better able to identify the plant traits that will help produce food that is going to be resilient to a changing climate. 

"It's all about fitness. We simply score: how do these plants respond to the stress? Which ones can cope with it, which ones suffer from it," said van de Zedde.

Researchers can use the data to see the DNA profiles linked to tolerance to certain stressors. They can then crossbreed varieties — one with a high yield and one that is robust, for example, to produce resilient offspring.

What's next for the research?

The goal is to fast forward evolution. The Dutch government and plant-breeding companies funding the research will decide which variants to continue to breed.

But Alan Pauls, Ph.D candidate in the university's Laboratory of Genetics, said the process has been met with criticism from some quarters.

"When you talk to the older generation, I definitely do feel like they don't trust it," he said. "The moment you talk about taking food or plants into a lab, immediately [what] you think about is GMO."

Genetically modified organisms, or GMOs, have had their genes changed artificially to make them take on a particular characteristic. One way it's done is to insert a gene from a different species, like bacteria, into a plant.

In the European Union, genetic modification is strictly legally regulated and requires rigorous safety checks. At Wageningen, just 5% of experiments involve genetically modified plants. Most focus on selecting existing traits through phenotyping, speeding up natural processes rather than creating new characteristics.

Pauls believes the argument that too much interference makes food artificial is outdated.

"Are we thinking that it's artificial because a machine is involved? Are we thinking that it's artificial because it's happening so fast, or it's happening in a lab?" he said. "I can still harvest rice with a sickle, but is it going to feed a billion people in time? No."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker



This article was adapted from a video in DW's Planet A series.
